rationale: 4 of 11 acceptance criteria are partial (AC#1, AC#4, AC#6, AC#8), blocking merge on their own; 9 code defects found including two auth gaps on read endpoints and an enum case mismatch that makes per-user grants invisible in list queries. One reachability was uncertain (CR-001, capped at major). 2 findings deferred as pre-existing (deferred backlog: code-review-deferred.md); 1 dismissed as noise.

business_review.item: AC#1 — POST /share with user_ids grants READ access; recipient can converse
business_review.notes: grant() writes Permission rows and is_shared_with gains per-user predicate. Conversation runtime owner-context forwarding not visible in diff.

business_review.item: AC#2 — Shared assistant appears in recipient accessible assistant list (VISIBLE_TO_USER scope)
AC#3 — Recipient cannot edit; Ability.can(WRITE) returns False
business_review.notes: Permission rows carry permission_level=READ. Existing WRITE-ability check is unchanged.

business_review.item: AC#4 — DELETE /share revokes access for listed users; subsequent reads return 403
business_review.notes: revoke() deletes Permission rows. Post-revocation 403 depends on is_shared_with returning False; not explicitly tested in new tests.

business_review.item: AC#5 — After revocation assistant no longer appears in revoked users' list
business_review.notes: per_user_grant_condition in list queries uses subquery; once Permission row is deleted the OR arm is false.

business_review.item: AC#6 — GET /sharable-users returns only is_external_user=False and is_active=True users
business_review.notes: aquery_active_users filters is_active=True; external-user filter applied in Python after DB fetch, not in SQL.

business_review.item: AC#7 — POST/DELETE /share by non-owner returns 403; no Permission row created or deleted
business_review.notes: _require_owner raises 403 before any DB writes; tests cover grant and revoke non-owner paths.

business_review.item: AC#8 — GET /shared-with returns current shared-with list for grant-access view
business_review.notes: Endpoint exists and calls list_shared_with. No ownership guard — any authenticated caller can query another owner's list.

business_review.item: AC#9 — Shared assistant appears in recipient personal project view
AC#10 — shared:true and per-user grants coexist without conflict
business_review.notes: is_shared_with evaluates project-shared first, then per-user grant; OR semantics in list queries are independent.

business_review.item: AC#11 — Recipient conversation executes against assistant's datasources without error
business_review.notes: Runtime context forwarding not in this diff; requires integration or conversation test evidence.

findings.title: is_shared_with queries DB with None resource_id
findings.problem: is_shared_with calls Permission.get_by_fields with resource_id=self.id, which may be None on an unsaved Assistant instance. Reachability from live call sites could not be confirmed (uncertain).
findings.impact: A DB query with resource_id=None may return unexpected rows or raise a database error; exact live reachability unconfirmed.
findings.recommendation: Add an early guard: if not self.id: return False before the Permission query block.

findings.title: ShareUsersRequest accepts empty user_ids list
findings.problem: user_ids: List[str] has no minimum-length constraint; POST /share and DELETE /share accept an empty list, iterate zero times, and return 200.
findings.impact: Silent no-ops are indistinguishable from a successful operation by clients; duplicate or empty calls cannot be rejected at the API boundary.
findings.recommendation: Add min_length=1 to the field: user_ids: List[str] = Field(..., min_length=1).

findings.title: GET /shared-with missing ownership guard
findings.problem: get_shared_with authenticates the caller but never verifies the caller owns the assistant; any authenticated user can query another owner's full grantee list.
findings.impact: User enumeration: an attacker with any valid assistant ID learns every user who has been granted access, leaking internal user identities and sharing relationships.
findings.recommendation: Load the assistant and call _require_owner (or inline the ownership check) before calling list_shared_with, matching the pattern on POST /share and DELETE /share.

findings.title: GET /sharable-users missing ownership guard
findings.problem: get_sharable_users authenticates the caller but never verifies ownership of the assistant; any authenticated user can pass any valid assistant ID to search the full internal user directory.
findings.impact: The internal user directory becomes searchable by any authenticated user via a valid assistant ID, exposing names, emails and usernames of all internal active users.
findings.recommendation: After Assistant.get_by_id, call _require_owner(user, assistant) before invoking search_sharable_users.

findings.title: Literal enum strings bypass DB enum case
findings.problem: per_user_grant_condition in both _get_non_global_base_condition and _filter_for_regular_user_visibility uses literal strings "assistant" and "user" in WHERE clauses. The DB resourcetype and principaltype PostgreSQL enums store uppercase labels (DATASOURCE, ASSISTANT, USER) per all migrations; lowercase literals match nothing.
findings.impact: Per-user grants are never matched in list queries: shared assistants do not appear in AC#2 and AC#9 visibility paths, making the entire sharing feature non-functional for list views.
findings.recommendation: Replace literal strings with enum member comparisons: Permission.resource_type == ResourceType.ASSISTANT and Permission.principal_type == PrincipalType.USER, letting SQLAlchemy resolve the DB representation. Alternatively verify that the column is stored as a VARCHAR with lowercase values and document it.

findings.title: grant() nested session breaks atomicity
findings.problem: grant() opens an explicit Session block, then each perm.save() call opens its own independent session and commits. Multiple Permission rows are written in separate transactions with no outer rollback boundary.
findings.impact: A failure after the first save leaves partial grants committed; concurrent requests may see inconsistent intermediate states during the grant sequence.
findings.recommendation: Pass the outer session into the save call, or perform the insert directly in the outer session: session.add(perm); session.commit() once after the loop.

findings.title: revoke() missing outer session context
findings.problem: revoke() calls perm.delete() for each uid with no enclosing Session; each delete opens and commits its own session. A mid-loop failure leaves some Permission rows deleted and others intact.
findings.impact: Partial revocation: some users lose access while others retain it without any error surfaced to the caller, making the access control state inconsistent.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the delete loop in a single Session block and call session.delete(perm) for each row, then session.commit() once at the end.

findings.title: search_sharable_users fetches all active users before filtering
findings.problem: aquery_active_users returns all active, non-deleted users regardless of user_type; the filter for external users is applied in Python after the full DB result set is fetched.
findings.impact: On large tenants, every sharable-user search transfers the full active-user table from DB to the application layer before stripping externals; AC#6 is only partially satisfied (external users are returned from DB and filtered in Python, not excluded at query time).
findings.recommendation: Add a user_type != config.EXTERNAL_USER_TYPE filter inside aquery_active_users (or as an additional WHERE clause in the call) so externals are excluded at the SQL level.

findings.title: Migration new_values uppercase contradicts Python model lowercase
findings.problem: The migration calls sync_enum_values with new_values=["DATASOURCE", "ASSISTANT"] (uppercase), while ResourceType.DATASOURCE = "datasource" and ResourceType.ASSISTANT = "assistant" (lowercase). alembic_postgresql_enum's sync_enum_values replaces the live enum values set; if the DB currently stores lowercase labels for existing datasource Permission rows, running this migration drops the lowercase values and breaks existing data.
findings.impact: Running the upgrade may make existing datasource Permission rows invalid (enum value no longer in the type), causing runtime errors on any code path that reads them; the downgrade similarly references ASSISTANT which may not exist if the column stores lowercase.
findings.recommendation: Audit which case the DB actually stores (SELECT DISTINCT resource_type FROM codemie.permissions); if lowercase, set new_values=["datasource", "assistant"]. Then align the Python enums and the repository literal strings to the same case. Document the canonical case in a comment.
